html:
Ancient Panjakent was a Sogdian town on the Zeravshan River in what is now Tajikistan, flourishing from about the 5th to the 8th century. Its ruins lie beside the modern town.

It was a small city of merchants and landowners, but its houses were richly painted. Soviet excavations from 1946 uncovered wall paintings of gods, banquets, battles and scenes from Persian epic tales later told in the Shahnameh, now mostly in the Hermitage and in Dushanbe. Its temples show the local mix of Zoroastrian and other cults.

Panjakent belonged to the world of Sogdian traders who ran much of the Silk Road trade, like the writers of the Ancient Letters. Its last ruler, Devashtich, rose against the Arabs and was killed in 722, and the city was abandoned by about 770. His papers survived on Mount Mugh.
